questions.q: Which single SQL statement does this course focus on almost exclusively?
options: DELETE
UPDATE
SELECT
INSERT
questions.explain: This course is about reading and investigating financial data, which is what SELECT is for. Statements that change data belong to data-loading work.

questions.q: Why does `WHERE vendor_site_id = NULL` silently return zero rows, even on rows that actually have a NULL there?
options: It raises a syntax error instead
Oracle automatically converts it to IS NULL behind the scenes
vendor_site_id can never actually be NULL
NULL is never equal to anything, including another NULL, so the `=` comparison is never true
questions.explain: NULL fails every equality comparison, including against itself, so `= NULL` never matches — the correct test is IS NULL.

questions.q: When does `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` take effect relative to `ORDER BY` in the same query?
options: Before ORDER BY runs
At the exact same time, with no defined order
FETCH FIRST cannot be combined with ORDER BY
After ORDER BY has already sorted the result
questions.explain: FETCH FIRST applies after the sort, which is why it reliably returns the correct top N rows.

questions.q: What does `ip.amount AS amount_on_this_check` return in the three-table join?
options: The total invoice amount, regardless of how many checks paid it
The portion of the invoice amount paid by this specific check
The remaining unpaid balance on the invoice
The supplier's total outstanding balance across all invoices
questions.explain: AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL.AMOUNT records the amount applied to the invoice by that specific check — not the full invoice total.

questions.q: Which column is used to join POZ_SUPPLIERS to AP_INVOICES_ALL?
options: SUPPLIER_ID
INVOICE_ID
VENDOR_ID
ACCOUNT_ID
questions.explain: Both tables carry a VENDOR_ID column — a naming leftover from when Oracle E-Business Suite called suppliers 'vendors'.

questions.q: Why does this course recommend LEFT OUTER JOIN over the legacy (+) syntax going forward?
options: Because (+) is no longer supported by any version of Oracle
Because LEFT OUTER JOIN is harder to read
Because (+) is easier to misplace, silently changing which side is kept, while LEFT OUTER JOIN is clearer and ANSI-standard
There is no real reason — both are equally recommended
questions.explain: LEFT OUTER JOIN is the clearer, ANSI-standard approach; (+) still works in Oracle but is more error-prone to write correctly.

questions.q: When you `GROUP BY vendor_id, invoice_month`, what determines whether two rows belong to the same group?
options: Only vendor_id needs to match
Both vendor_id AND invoice_month must match — it's the combination that defines a group
Only invoice_month needs to match
Rows are never grouped together if there are two GROUP BY columns
questions.explain: With multiple GROUP BY columns, Oracle creates one group per distinct combination of all listed columns.

options: The sum of a numeric column
The number of distinct values in a column
The number of NULL values only
The number of rows
questions.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows, regardless of what values any particular column holds.

questions.q: In `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY vendor_id ORDER BY check_date)`, what does PARTITION BY do?
options: It deletes rows for other suppliers
It sorts the entire result set by vendor_id
It has no effect unless combined with HAVING
It restarts the running calculation for each distinct vendor_id, similar in spirit to GROUP BY but without collapsing rows
questions.explain: PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for the window calculation, restarting the running total at each new group, while all rows remain in the output.

questions.q: What does Oracle call the set-difference operator that other databases like SQL Server call EXCEPT?
options: SUBTRACT
DIFF
MINUS
REMOVE
questions.explain: Oracle has traditionally called this operator MINUS; EXCEPT was added as a newer alias only in Oracle 21c.

questions.q: What does the correlated subquery `WHERE i1.invoice_amount > (SELECT AVG(i2.invoice_amount) FROM ap_invoices_all i2 WHERE i2.vendor_id = i1.vendor_id)` find?
options: Invoices priced above average for their own specific supplier
Invoices priced above the overall average across all suppliers
Every invoice in the table, regardless of amount
Only the single most expensive invoice in the entire table
questions.explain: Because the inner AVG is filtered to i1's own vendor_id, the comparison is against that specific supplier's average, not the company-wide average.

questions.q: Why doesn't NOT EXISTS have the same NULL problem as NOT IN?
options: NOT EXISTS ignores NULL values automatically by converting them to empty strings
NOT EXISTS only tests whether a matching row exists via its WHERE condition, so a stray NULL elsewhere in the subquery's result doesn't corrupt the comparison
NOT EXISTS cannot be used with any subquery that references NULL-able columns
They behave identically and both have the same NULL risk
questions.explain: NOT EXISTS is a presence test based on the join condition inside the subquery, not a value-list comparison, so NULLs elsewhere don't break it.

questions.q: In the overpayment check, why does HAVING use `SUM(ip.amount) > i.invoice_amount` instead of `<> 0`?
options: There is no difference — both produce identical results
Because only the overpayment direction (paid more than invoiced) is being flagged here, which is operationally more urgent than underpayment
Because `<> 0` is invalid syntax in a HAVING clause
Because `>` always runs faster than `<>`
questions.explain: The check specifically targets one direction of discrepancy — paying more than was invoiced — rather than any mismatch in either direction.

questions.q: How does a 'trace' query differ from a 'list' query?
options: A trace query never uses JOINs
A list query can only return one row
A trace query starts from one specific, known record and walks backward through joins, rather than starting from a condition and returning all matches
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: A trace/audit-trail query begins with a known record (like a specific check number) and follows the joins back to its origin, while a list query filters by a condition to return all matching rows.

questions.q: Why does the final query filter on `ps.amount_remaining > 10000` rather than `i.invoice_amount > 10000`?
options: There is no difference between the two columns
Because invoice_amount does not exist on AP_INVOICES_ALL
Because amount_remaining is always identical to invoice_amount
Because a partially-paid invoice could have started above $10,000 but have less remaining outstanding now, and "over $10,000" should mean the outstanding balance
questions.explain: The business question is about outstanding exposure, which AMOUNT_REMAINING reflects after partial payments — INVOICE_AMOUNT reflects only the original total.

options: Any WHERE condition that uses the equals sign
A condition that always returns zero rows
A predicate that only works in HAVING, never WHERE
A WHERE condition the database can use an index to satisfy directly, without wrapping the column in a function
questions.explain: Sargable conditions let the database leverage an index directly on the stored column values, rather than needing to compute something on every row first.

options: Whether an accounting period is open, closed, or permanently closed
The total dollar amount posted in a period
The supplier associated with a period
The exchange rate used for a period
questions.explain: CLOSING_STATUS tracks a period's state (e.g., open, closed, permanently closed), which is essential to check before processing transactions into it.

questions.q: What reconciliation pattern does Investigation 2 (unapplied cash by customer) reuse from Lesson 21?
options: LEFT OUTER JOIN plus an NVL-guarded difference, filtered with HAVING <> 0
CASE-based aging buckets
ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer
The MINUS set operator
questions.explain: Investigation 2 directly reapplies Lesson 21's reconciliation pattern: outer join, NVL-guard the aggregate, then HAVING the difference not equal to zero.
